It addressed the [fall of man](/wiki/Fall_of_man "Fall of man"), including the temptation of [Adam and Eve](/wiki/Adam_and_Eve "Adam and Eve") by the [fallen angel](/wiki/Fallen_angel "Fallen angel") [Satan](/wiki/Satan "Satan"), and [God](/wiki/God "God")'s expulsion of them from the [Garden of Eden](/wiki/Garden_of_Eden "Garden of Eden"). *Paradise Lost* elevated Milton's reputation as one of history's greatest poets.[[1]](#cite_note-John_Milton-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2) He also served as a civil servant for the [Commonwealth of England](/wiki/Commonwealth_of_England "Commonwealth of England") under its [Council of State](/wiki/English_Council_of_State "English Council of State") and later under [Oliver Cromwell](/wiki/Oliver_Cromwell "Oliver Cromwell").

Milton achieved fame and recognition during his lifetime. His celebrated *[Areopagitica](/wiki/Areopagitica "Areopagitica")* (1644) condemning [pre-publication censorship](/wiki/Prior_restraint "Prior restraint") is among history's most influential and impassioned defences of [freedom of speech](/wiki/Freedom_of_speech "Freedom of speech") and [freedom of the press](/wiki/Freedom_of_the_press "Freedom of the press"). His desire for freedom extended beyond his philosophy and was reflected in his style, which included his introduction of new words to the English language, coined from [Latin](/wiki/Latin "Latin") and [Ancient Greek](/wiki/Ancient_Greek "Ancient Greek"). He was the first modern writer to employ unrhymed verse outside of the theatre or translations.

Milton is described as the "greatest English author" by his biographer [William Hayley](/wiki/William_Hayley "William Hayley"),[[3]](#cite_note-3) and he remains generally regarded "as one of the preeminent writers in the [English language](/wiki/English_literature "English literature")",[[4]](#cite_note-4) though critical reception has oscillated in the centuries since his death, often on account of his [republicanism](/wiki/Republicanism_in_the_United_Kingdom#Commonwealth_of_England "Republicanism in the United Kingdom"). [Samuel Johnson](/wiki/Samuel_Johnson "Samuel Johnson") praised *Paradise Lost* as "a poem which ... with respect to design may claim the first place, and with respect to performance, the second, among the productions of the human mind", though he (a [Tory](/wiki/Tories_(British_political_party) "Tories (British political party)")) described Milton's politics as those of an "acrimonious and surly republican".[[5]](#cite_note-Works-5) Milton was revered by poets such as [William Blake](/wiki/William_Blake "William Blake"), [William Wordsworth](/wiki/William_Wordsworth "William Wordsworth"), and [Thomas Hardy](/wiki/Thomas_Hardy "Thomas Hardy").

Phases of Milton's life parallel the major historical and political divisions in [Stuart England](/wiki/House_of_Stuart "House of Stuart") at the time. In his early years, Milton studied at [Christ's College](/wiki/Christ%27s_College,_Cambridge "Christ's College, Cambridge") at the [University of Cambridge](/wiki/University_of_Cambridge "University of Cambridge"), and then travelled, wrote poetry mostly for private circulation, and launched a career as [pamphleteer](/wiki/Pamphleteer "Pamphleteer") and [publicist](/wiki/Publicist "Publicist") under [Charles I](/wiki/Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England")'s increasingly autocratic rule and Britain's breakdown into constitutional confusion and ultimately civil war. He was once considered dangerously radical and heretical, but he contributed to a seismic shift in accepted public opinions during his life that ultimately elevated him to public office in England. The [Restoration](/wiki/Stuart_Restoration "Stuart Restoration") of 1660 and his loss of vision later deprived Milton of much of his public platform, but he used the period to develop many of his major works.

Milton's views developed from extensive reading, travel, and experience that began with his days as a student at the University of Cambridge in the 1620s and continued through the [English Civil War](/wiki/English_Civil_War "English Civil War"), which started in 1642 and continued until 1651.[[6]](#cite_note-6) By the time of his death in 1674, Milton was impoverished and on the margins of English intellectual life but famous throughout Europe and unrepentant for political choices that placed him at odds with governing authorities.

Milton is widely regarded as one of the greatest poets in English literature, though his oeuvre has drawn criticism from notable figures, including [T. S. Eliot](/wiki/T._S._Eliot "T. S. Eliot") and [Joseph Addison](/wiki/Joseph_Addison "Joseph Addison"). According to some scholars, Milton was second in influence to none but [William Shakespeare](/wiki/William_Shakespeare "William Shakespeare"). In one of his books, Johnson praised him for having the power of "displaying the vast, illuminating the splendid, enforcing the awful, darkening the gloomy and aggravating the dreadful".

Early life and education
------------------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Milton&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Main article: [Early life of John Milton](/wiki/Early_life_of_John_Milton "Early life of John Milton")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/df/The_poet_and_statesman_John_Milton_was_born_1608_in_Bread_Street.jpg/250px-The_poet_and_statesman_John_Milton_was_born_1608_in_Bread_Street.jpg)](/wiki/File:The_poet_and_statesman_John_Milton_was_born_1608_in_Bread_Street.jpg)

Blue plaque on 1 [Bread Street](/wiki/Bread_Street "Bread Street"), [London](/wiki/London "London"), commemorating Milton's birthplace

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fc/John_Milton_portrait.jpg/250px-John_Milton_portrait.jpg)](/wiki/File:John_Milton_portrait.jpg)

Portrait of Milton at age 10 in [Milton's Cottage](/wiki/Milton%27s_Cottage "Milton's Cottage"), [Chalfont St Giles](/wiki/Chalfont_St_Giles "Chalfont St Giles"), Buckinghamshire, painted by [Cornelis Janssens van Ceulen](/wiki/Cornelis_Janssens_van_Ceulen "Cornelis Janssens van Ceulen")

John Milton was born in [Bread Street](/wiki/Bread_Street "Bread Street"), London, on 9 December 1608, the son of composer [John Milton](/wiki/John_Milton_(composer) "John Milton (composer)") and his wife Sarah Jeffrey. The senior John Milton (1562–1647) moved to London around 1583 after being disinherited by his devout [Catholic](/wiki/Catholic_Church "Catholic Church") father Richard Milton for embracing [Protestantism](/wiki/Protestantism "Protestantism").[[7]](#cite_note-:3-7) In London, the senior John Milton married Sarah Jeffrey (1572–1637) and found lasting financial success as a [scrivener](/wiki/Scrivener "Scrivener").[[8]](#cite_note-Forsyth16-8) He lived in and worked from a house in [Cheapside](/wiki/Cheapside "Cheapside") at Bread Street, where the [Mermaid Tavern](/wiki/Mermaid_Tavern "Mermaid Tavern") was located. The elder Milton was noted for his skill as a composer of music, and this talent left his son with a lifelong appreciation for music and friendships with musicians such as [Henry Lawes](/wiki/Henry_Lawes "Henry Lawes").[[9]](#cite_note-9)

The prosperity of Milton's father allowed his eldest son to obtain a private tutor, [Thomas Young](/wiki/Thomas_Young_(1587%E2%80%931655) "Thomas Young (1587–1655)"), a Scottish Presbyterian with an [MA](/wiki/Master_of_Arts "Master of Arts") from the [University of St Andrews](/wiki/University_of_St_Andrews "University of St Andrews"). Young's influence also served as the poet's introduction to religious radicalism.[[10]](#cite_note-10) After Young's tutorship, Milton attended [St Paul's School](/wiki/St_Paul%27s_School_(London) "St Paul's School (London)") in London, where he began the study of Latin and Greek; the classical languages left an imprint on both his poetry and prose in English (he also wrote in Latin and Italian).

Milton's first datable compositions are two psalms written at age 15 at [Long Bennington](/wiki/Long_Bennington "Long Bennington"). One contemporary source is *[Brief Lives](/wiki/Brief_Lives "Brief Lives")* of [John Aubrey](/wiki/John_Aubrey "John Aubrey"), an uneven compilation including first-hand reports. In the work, Aubrey quotes Christopher, Milton's younger brother: "When he was young, he studied very hard and sat up very late, commonly till twelve or one o'clock at night". Aubrey adds, "His complexion exceeding faire—he was so faire that they called him the Lady of Christ's College."[[11]](#cite_note-OLD-11)

In 1625, Milton gained entry to [Christ's College](/wiki/Christ%27s_College,_Cambridge "Christ's College, Cambridge") at the [University of Cambridge](/wiki/University_of_Cambridge "University of Cambridge"), where he graduated with a [BA](/wiki/Bachelor_of_Arts "Bachelor of Arts") in 1629,[[12]](#cite_note-12) ranking fourth of 24 honours graduates that year in the University of Cambridge.[[13]](#cite_note-13) Preparing, at that time, to become an [Anglican](/wiki/Anglicanism "Anglicanism") priest, he stayed on at Cambridge where he received his [MA](/wiki/Master_of_Arts "Master of Arts") on 3 July 1632.

Milton may have been [rusticated](/wiki/Rustication_(academia) "Rustication (academia)") (suspended) in his first year at Cambridge for quarrelling with his tutor, Bishop [William Chappell](/wiki/William_Chappell_(bishop) "William Chappell (bishop)"). He was certainly at home in London in the Lent Term 1626; there he wrote *Elegia Prima*, his first Latin [elegy](/wiki/Elegy "Elegy"), to Charles Diodati, a friend from St Paul's. Based on remarks of [John Aubrey](/wiki/John_Aubrey "John Aubrey"), Chappell "whipt" Milton.[[11]](#cite_note-OLD-11) This story is now disputed, though certainly Milton disliked Chappell.[[14]](#cite_note-14) Historian [Christopher Hill](/wiki/Christopher_Hill_(historian) "Christopher Hill (historian)") notes that Milton was apparently rusticated and that the differences between Chappell and Milton may have been either religious or personal.[[15]](#cite_note-15) It is also possible that, like [Isaac Newton](/wiki/Isaac_Newton "Isaac Newton") four decades later, Milton was sent home from Cambridge because of the [plague](/wiki/Plague_(disease) "Plague (disease)"), which afflicted Cambridge in 1625.

At Cambridge, Milton was on good terms with [Edward King](/wiki/Edward_King_(British_poet) "Edward King (British poet)"); he later dedicated "[Lycidas](/wiki/Lycidas "Lycidas")" to him. Milton also befriended theologian [Roger Williams](/wiki/Roger_Williams "Roger Williams"), tutoring Williams in [Hebrew](/wiki/Hebrew_language "Hebrew language") in exchange for lessons in [Dutch](/wiki/Dutch_language "Dutch language").[[16]](#cite_note-16) Despite developing a reputation for poetic skill and general erudition, Milton suffered from alienation among his peers during his time at Cambridge. Having once watched his fellow students attempting comedy on the college stage, he later observed, "they thought themselves gallant men, and I thought them fools".[[17]](#cite_note-17)

Milton also was disdainful of the university curriculum, which consisted of stilted formal debates conducted in Latin on abstruse topics.[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] His own corpus is not devoid of humour, notably his sixth [prolusion](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/prolusion "wikt:prolusion") and his epitaphs on the death of [Thomas Hobson](/wiki/Thomas_Hobson_(postal_carrier) "Thomas Hobson (postal carrier)"). While at Cambridge, he wrote some of his well-known shorter English poems, including "On the Morning of Christ's Nativity", "Epitaph on the admirable Dramaticke Poet, W. Shakespeare" (his first poem to appear in print), *[L'Allegro](/wiki/L%27Allegro "L'Allegro")*, and *[Il Penseroso](/wiki/Il_Penseroso "Il Penseroso")*.

Study, poetry, and travel
-------------------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Milton&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Study, poetry, and travel")]

Further information: [Early life of John Milton](/wiki/Early_life_of_John_Milton "Early life of John Milton")

> It appears in all his writings that he had the usual concomitant of great abilities, a lofty and steady confidence in himself, perhaps not without some contempt of others; for scarcely any man ever wrote so much, and praised so few. Of his praise he was very frugal; as he set its value high, and considered his mention of a name as a security against the waste of time, and a certain preservative from oblivion.[[18]](#cite_note-18)

— [Samuel Johnson](/wiki/Samuel_Johnson "Samuel Johnson"), *[Lives of the Most Eminent English Poets](/wiki/Lives_of_the_Most_Eminent_English_Poets "Lives of the Most Eminent English Poets")*

After receiving his MA, Milton moved to [Hammersmith](/wiki/Hammersmith "Hammersmith"), his father's new home since the previous year. He also lived at [Horton](/wiki/Horton,_Berkshire "Horton, Berkshire"), Berkshire, from 1635 and undertook six years of self-directed private study. Hill argues that this was not retreating into a rural idyll; Hammersmith was then a "suburban village" falling into the orbit of London, and even Horton was becoming deforested and suffered from the plague.[[19]](#cite_note-19) He read both ancient and modern works of theology, philosophy, history, politics, literature, and science in preparation for a prospective poetical career. Milton's intellectual development can be charted via entries in his [commonplace book](/wiki/Commonplace_book "Commonplace book") (like a scrapbook), now in the [British Library](/wiki/British_Library "British Library"). As a result of such intensive study, Milton is considered to be among the most learned of all English poets. In addition to his years of private study, Milton had command of Latin, Greek, Hebrew, French, Spanish, and Italian from his school and undergraduate days; he also added Old English to his linguistic repertoire in the 1650s while researching his *History of Britain*, and probably acquired proficiency in Dutch soon after.[[20]](#cite_note-20)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f9/John_Milton_plaque_Berkyn_Manor_Farm_Horton.JPG/250px-John_Milton_plaque_Berkyn_Manor_Farm_Horton.JPG)](/wiki/File:John_Milton_plaque_Berkyn_Manor_Farm_Horton.JPG)

Commemorative blue plaque 'John Milton lived here 1632–1638' at Berkyn Manor Farm, [Horton, Berkshire](/wiki/Horton,_Berkshire "Horton, Berkshire")

Milton continued to write poetry during this period of study; his *[Arcades](/wiki/Arcades_(Milton) "Arcades (Milton)")* and *[Comus](/wiki/Comus_(John_Milton) "Comus (John Milton)")* were both commissioned for [masques](/wiki/Masques "Masques") composed for noble patrons, connections of the Egerton family, and performed in 1632 and 1634 respectively. *Comus* argues for the virtuousness of [temperance](/wiki/Temperance_(virtue) "Temperance (virtue)") and [chastity](/wiki/Chastity "Chastity"). He contributed his [pastoral](/wiki/Pastoral "Pastoral") [elegy](/wiki/Elegy "Elegy") *[Lycidas](/wiki/Lycidas "Lycidas")* to a memorial collection for one of his fellow students at Cambridge. Drafts of these poems are preserved in Milton's poetry notebook, known as the Trinity Manuscript, because it is now kept at [Trinity College](/wiki/Trinity_College,_Cambridge "Trinity College, Cambridge"), Cambridge. It was [Charles Mason](/wiki/Charles_Mason_(academic_and_clergyman) "Charles Mason (academic and clergyman)") who made the extraordinary discovery, in the library of Trinity College, of *a packet of thirty loose and tattered folio leaves, almost covered with the handwriting of Milton*.[[21]](#cite_note-Atlantic-21) It is thought that Mason recognised the nature of this material around 1735 and the loose-leaf sheets were bound for the first time in 1736; the Trinity Manuscript has been described as *"the chief treasure of Trinity Library"*.[[21]](#cite_note-Atlantic-21)

In May 1638, accompanied by a manservant, Milton embarked upon a tour of France and Italy for 15 months that lasted until July or August 1639.[[22]](#cite_note-22) His travels supplemented his study with new and direct experiences of artistic and religious traditions, especially Roman Catholicism. He met famous theorists and intellectuals of the time and was able to display his poetic skills. For specific details of what happened within Milton's "[grand tour](/wiki/Grand_tour "Grand tour")", there appears to be just one [primary source](/wiki/Primary_source "Primary source"): Milton's own *[Defensio Secunda](/wiki/Defensio_Secunda "Defensio Secunda")*. There are other records, including some letters and some references in his other prose tracts, but the bulk of the information about the tour comes from a work that, according to [Barbara Lewalski](/wiki/Barbara_Lewalski "Barbara Lewalski"), "was not intended as autobiography but as rhetoric, designed to emphasise his sterling reputation with the learned of Europe."[[23]](#cite_note-23)

He first went to [Calais](/wiki/Calais "Calais") and then on to Paris, riding horseback, with a letter from diplomat [Henry Wotton](/wiki/Henry_Wotton "Henry Wotton") to ambassador [John Scudamore](/wiki/John_Scudamore_(ambassador) "John Scudamore (ambassador)"). Through Scudamore, Milton met [Hugo Grotius](/wiki/Hugo_Grotius "Hugo Grotius"), a Dutch law philosopher, playwright, and poet. Milton left France soon after this meeting. He travelled south from [Nice](/wiki/Nice,_France "Nice, France") to [Genoa](/wiki/Genoa "Genoa"), and then to [Livorno](/wiki/Livorno "Livorno") and [Pisa](/wiki/Pisa "Pisa"). He reached Florence in July 1638. While there, Milton enjoyed many of the sites and structures of the city. His candour of manner and erudite neo-Latin poetry earned him friends in Florentine intellectual circles, and he met the astronomer [Galileo](/wiki/Galileo "Galileo") who was under [house arrest](/wiki/House_arrest "House arrest") at [Arcetri](/wiki/Arcetri "Arcetri"), as well as others.[[24]](#cite_note-24) Milton probably visited the Florentine Academy and the [Accademia della Crusca](/wiki/Accademia_della_Crusca "Accademia della Crusca") along with smaller academies in the area, including the [Apatisti](/wiki/Accademia_degli_Apatisti "Accademia degli Apatisti") and the [Svogliati](/wiki/Svogliati "Svogliati").

> In [Florence], which I have always admired above all others because of the elegance, not just of its tongue, but also of its wit, I lingered for about two months. There I at once became the friend of many gentlemen eminent in rank and learning, whose private academies I frequented—a Florentine institution which deserves great praise not only for promoting humane studies but also for encouraging friendly intercourse.[[25]](#cite_note-25)

— Milton's account of Florence in *Defensio Secunda*

He left Florence in September to continue to Rome. With the connections from Florence, Milton was able to have easy access to Rome's intellectual society. His poetic abilities impressed those like Giovanni Salzilli, who praised Milton within an epigram. In late October, Milton attended a dinner given by the [English College, Rome](/wiki/English_College,_Rome "English College, Rome"), despite his dislike for the [Society of Jesus](/wiki/Society_of_Jesus "Society of Jesus"), meeting English Catholics who were also guests—theologian [Henry Holden](/wiki/Henry_Holden_(theologian) "Henry Holden (theologian)") and the poet [Patrick Cary](/wiki/Patrick_Cary "Patrick Cary").[[26]](#cite_note-26) He also attended musical events, including oratorios, operas, and melodramas. Milton left for [Naples](/wiki/Naples "Naples") toward the end of November, where he stayed only for a month because of the Spanish control.[[27]](#cite_note-27) During that time, he was introduced to [Giovanni Battista Manso](/wiki/Giovanni_Battista_Manso "Giovanni Battista Manso"), patron to both [Torquato Tasso](/wiki/Torquato_Tasso "Torquato Tasso") and to [Giambattista Marino](/wiki/Giambattista_Marino "Giambattista Marino").[[28]](#cite_note-28)

Originally, Milton wanted to leave Naples in order to travel to [Sicily](/wiki/Sicily "Sicily") and then on to Greece, but he returned to England during the summer of 1639 because of what he claimed in *Defensio Secunda*[[29]](#cite_note-29) were "sad tidings of civil war in England."[[30]](#cite_note-30) Matters became more complicated when Milton received word that his childhood friend Diodati had died. Milton in fact stayed another seven months on the continent and spent time at [Geneva](/wiki/Geneva "Geneva") with Diodati's uncle after he returned to Rome. In *Defensio Secunda*, Milton proclaimed that he was warned against a return to Rome because of his frankness about religion, but he stayed in the city for two months and was able to experience [Carnival](/wiki/Carnival "Carnival") and meet [Lukas Holste](/wiki/Lukas_Holste "Lukas Holste"), a Vatican librarian who guided Milton through its collection. He was introduced to Cardinal [Francesco Barberini](/wiki/Francesco_Barberini_(1597%E2%80%931679) "Francesco Barberini (1597–1679)") who invited Milton to an opera hosted by the Cardinal. Around March, Milton travelled once again to Florence, staying there for two months, attending further meetings of the academies, and spending time with friends. After leaving Florence, he travelled through Lucca, Bologna, and Ferrara before coming to [Venice](/wiki/Venice "Venice"). In Venice, Milton was exposed to a model of Republicanism, later important in his political writings, but he soon found another model when he travelled to Geneva. From Switzerland, Milton travelled to Paris and then to Calais before finally arriving back in England in either July or August 1639.[[31]](#cite_note-31)

Civil war, prose tracts, and marriage
-------------------------------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Milton&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Civil war, prose tracts, and marriage")]

Main article: [Milton's antiprelatical tracts](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ed/Areopagitica_bridwell.jpg/250px-Areopagitica_bridwell.jpg)](/wiki/File:Areopagitica_bridwell.jpg)

Title page of the 1644 edition of *[Areopagitica](/wiki/Areopagitica "Areopagitica")*

On returning to England where the [Bishops' Wars](/wiki/Bishops%27_Wars "Bishops' Wars") presaged further armed conflict, Milton began to write prose [tracts](/wiki/Tract_(literature) "Tract (literature)") against [episcopacy](/wiki/Episcopacy "Episcopacy"), in the service of the [Puritan](/wiki/Puritans "Puritans") and [Parliamentary](/wiki/Long_Parliament "Long Parliament") cause. Milton's first foray into polemics was *Of Reformation touching Church Discipline in England* (1641), followed by *Of Prelatical Episcopacy*, the two defences of [Smectymnuus](/wiki/Smectymnuus "Smectymnuus") (a group of Presbyterian divines named from their initials; the "TY" belonged to Milton's old tutor Thomas Young), and *[The Reason of Church-Government Urged against Prelaty](/wiki/The_Reason_of_Church-Government_Urged_against_Prelaty "The Reason of Church-Government Urged against Prelaty")*. He vigorously attacked the High-church party of the Church of England and their leader [William Laud](/wiki/William_Laud "William Laud"), [Archbishop of Canterbury](/wiki/Archbishop_of_Canterbury "Archbishop of Canterbury"), with frequent passages of real eloquence lighting up the rough controversial style of the period, and deploying a wide knowledge of church history.

He was supported by his father's investments, but Milton became a private schoolmaster at this time, educating his nephews and other children of the well-to-do. This experience and discussions with educational reformer [Samuel Hartlib](/wiki/Samuel_Hartlib "Samuel Hartlib") led him to write his short tract *[Of Education](/wiki/Of_Education "Of Education")* in 1644, urging a reform of the national universities.

In June 1642, Milton paid a visit to the manor house at [Forest Hill, Oxfordshire](/wiki/Forest_Hill,_Oxfordshire "Forest Hill, Oxfordshire"), and, aged 34, married the 17-year-old Mary Powell.[[32]](#cite_note-ODNB_Milton-32)[[33]](#cite_note-33) The marriage got off to a poor start as Mary did not adapt to Milton's austere lifestyle or get along with his nephews. Milton found her intellectually unsatisfying and disliked the royalist views she had absorbed from her family. It is also speculated that she refused to consummate the marriage. Mary soon returned home to her parents and did not come back until 1645, partly because of the outbreak of the [Civil War](/wiki/First_English_Civil_War "First English Civil War").[[32]](#cite_note-ODNB_Milton-32)

In the meantime, her desertion prompted Milton to publish [a series of pamphlets](/wiki/Milton%27s_divorce_tracts "Milton's divorce tracts") over the next three years arguing for the legality and morality of divorce beyond grounds of adultery. ([Anna Beer](/wiki/Anna_Beer "Anna Beer"), author of a 2008 biography of Milton, points to a lack of evidence and the dangers of cynicism in urging that it was not necessarily the case that the private life so animated the public polemicising.) In 1643, Milton had a brush with the authorities over these writings, in parallel with [Hezekiah Woodward](/wiki/Hezekiah_Woodward "Hezekiah Woodward"), who had more trouble.[[34]](#cite_note-34) It was the hostile response accorded the divorce tracts that spurred Milton to write *[Areopagitica; A speech of Mr. John Milton for the Liberty of Unlicenc'd Printing, to the Parlament of England](/wiki/Areopagitica "Areopagitica")*, his celebrated attack on pre-printing censorship. In *Areopagitica*, Milton aligns himself with the [parliamentary cause](/wiki/Roundhead "Roundhead"), and he also begins to synthesize the ideal of neo-Roman liberty with that of Christian liberty. Milton also courted another woman during this time; we know nothing of her except that her name was Davis and she turned him down. However, it was enough to induce Mary Powell into returning to him which she did unexpectedly by begging him to take her back. They had two daughters in quick succession following their reconciliation.[[35]](#cite_note-35)[[36]](#cite_note-36)

Secretary for Foreign Tongues
-----------------------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Milton&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Secretary for Foreign Tongues")]

With the Parliamentary victory in the Civil War, Milton used his pen in defence of the republican principles represented by the Commonwealth.[[37]](#cite_note-37) *[The Tenure of Kings and Magistrates](/wiki/The_Tenure_of_Kings_and_Magistrates "The Tenure of Kings and Magistrates")* (1649) defended the right of the people to hold their rulers to account, and implicitly sanctioned the [regicide](/wiki/Regicide "Regicide"); Milton's political reputation got him appointed Secretary for Foreign Tongues by the Council of State in March 1649. His main job description was to compose the English Republic's foreign correspondence in [Latin](/wiki/Neo-Latin "Neo-Latin") and other languages, but he also was called upon to produce propaganda for the regime and to serve as a censor.[[38]](#cite_note-38)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/61/19_York_Street%2C_Westminster_%281848%29.jpg/250px-19_York_Street%2C_Westminster_%281848%29.jpg)](/wiki/File:19_York_Street,_Westminster_(1848).jpg)

The back of no 19 York Street (1848). In 1651, Milton moved into a "pretty garden-house" in [Petty France, Westminster](/wiki/Petty_France,_Westminster "Petty France, Westminster"). He lived there until the Restoration. Later it became No. 19 York Street, belonged to [Jeremy Bentham](/wiki/Jeremy_Bentham "Jeremy Bentham"), was occupied successively by [James Mill](/wiki/James_Mill "James Mill") and [William Hazlitt](/wiki/William_Hazlitt "William Hazlitt"), and finally was demolished in 1877.[[39]](#cite_note-39)

In October 1649, he published *[Eikonoklastes](/wiki/Eikonoklastes "Eikonoklastes")*, an explicit defence of the regicide, in response to the *[Eikon Basilike](/wiki/Eikon_Basilike "Eikon Basilike")*, a phenomenal best-seller popularly attributed to Charles I that portrayed the King as an innocent Christian [martyr](/wiki/Martyr "Martyr"). A month later the exiled [Charles II](/wiki/Charles_II_of_England "Charles II of England") and his party published the defence of monarchy *Defensio Regia pro Carolo Primo*, written by leading humanist [Claudius Salmasius](/wiki/Claudius_Salmasius "Claudius Salmasius"). By January of the following year, Milton was ordered to write a defence of the English people by the [Council of State](/wiki/English_Council_of_State "English Council of State"). Milton worked more slowly than usual, given the European audience and the English Republic's desire to establish diplomatic and cultural legitimacy, as he drew on the learning marshalled by his years of study to compose a riposte.

On 24 February 1652, Milton published his Latin defence of the English people *[Defensio pro Populo Anglicano](/wiki/Defensio_pro_Populo_Anglicano "Defensio pro Populo Anglicano")*, also known as the *First Defence*. Milton's pure Latin prose and evident learning exemplified in the *First Defence* quickly made him a European reputation, and the work ran to numerous editions.[[40]](#cite_note-40) He addressed his *Sonnet 16* to 'The Lord Generall Cromwell in May 1652' beginning "Cromwell, our chief of men ...", although it was not published until 1654.[[41]](#cite_note-41)

In 1654, Milton completed the second defence of the English nation *Defensio secunda* in response to an anonymous Royalist tract *"Regii Sanguinis Clamor ad Coelum Adversus Parricidas Anglicanos"* [The Cry of the Royal Blood to Heaven Against the English Parricides], a work that made many personal attacks on Milton.[[42]](#cite_note-42) The second defence praised [Oliver Cromwell](/wiki/Oliver_Cromwell "Oliver Cromwell"), now Lord Protector, while exhorting him to remain true to the principles of the Revolution. [Alexander Morus](/wiki/Alexander_Morus "Alexander Morus"), to whom Milton wrongly attributed the *Clamor* (in fact by [Peter du Moulin](/wiki/Peter_du_Moulin "Peter du Moulin")), published an attack on Milton, in response to which Milton published the autobiographical *Defensio pro se* in 1655. Milton held the appointment of Secretary for Foreign Tongues to the Commonwealth Council of State until 1660, although after he had become totally blind, most of the work was done by his deputies, [Georg Rudolph Wecklein](/w/index.php?title=Georg_Rudolph_Wecklein&action=edit&redlink=1 "Georg Rudolph Wecklein (page does not exist)"), then [Philip Meadows](/wiki/Philip_Meadows_(died_1718) "Philip Meadows (died 1718)"), and from 1657 by the poet [Andrew Marvell](/wiki/Andrew_Marvell "Andrew Marvell").[[43]](#cite_note-43)

By 1652, Milton had become totally blind;[[44]](#cite_note-44) the cause of his blindness is debated but bilateral [retinal detachment](/wiki/Retinal_detachment "Retinal detachment") or [glaucoma](/wiki/Glaucoma "Glaucoma") are most likely.[[45]](#cite_note-pmid18168884-45) His blindness forced him to dictate his [verse](/wiki/Verse_(poetry) "Verse (poetry)") and prose to [amanuenses](/wiki/Amanuensis "Amanuensis") who copied them out for him; one of these was Andrew Marvell. One of his best-known sonnets, "[When I Consider How My Light is Spent](/wiki/When_I_Consider_How_My_Light_is_Spent "When I Consider How My Light is Spent")," titled by a later editor, [John Newton](/wiki/John_Newton "John Newton"), "On His Blindness," is presumed to date from this period.[[46]](#cite_note-46)

The Restoration
---------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Milton&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: The Restoration")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d8/John_Milton_1.jpg/250px-John_Milton_1.jpg)](/wiki/File:John_Milton_1.jpg)

[Engraving](/wiki/Engraving "Engraving") by [William Faithorne](/wiki/William_Faithorne "William Faithorne"), 1670

Cromwell's death in 1658 caused the English Republic to collapse into feuding military and political factions. Milton, however, stubbornly clung to the beliefs that had originally inspired him to write for the Commonwealth. In 1659, he published *[A Treatise of Civil Power](/wiki/A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power "A Treatise of Civil Power")*, attacking the concept of a state-dominated church (the position known as [Erastianism](/wiki/Erastianism "Erastianism")), as well as *Considerations touching the likeliest means to remove hirelings*, denouncing corrupt practises in church governance. As the Republic disintegrated, Milton wrote several proposals to retain a non-monarchical government against the wishes of parliament, soldiers, and the people.[[47]](#cite_note-47)[[48]](#cite_note-48)

* *A Letter to a Friend, Concerning the Ruptures of the Commonwealth*, written in October 1659, was a response to [General Lambert](/wiki/John_Lambert_(general) "John Lambert (general)")'s recent dissolution of the [Rump Parliament](/wiki/Rump_Parliament "Rump Parliament").
* *Proposals of certain expedients for the preventing of a civil war now feared*, written in November 1659.
* *[The Ready and Easy Way to Establishing a Free Commonwealth](/wiki/The_Ready_and_Easy_Way_to_Establishing_a_Free_Commonwealth "The Ready and Easy Way to Establishing a Free Commonwealth")*, in two editions, responded to [General Monck](/wiki/George_Monck,_1st_Duke_of_Albemarle "George Monck, 1st Duke of Albemarle")'s march towards London to restore the [Long Parliament](/wiki/Long_Parliament "Long Parliament") (which led to the restoration of the monarchy). The work is an impassioned, bitter, and futile [jeremiad](/wiki/Jeremiad "Jeremiad") damning the English people for backsliding from the cause of [liberty](/wiki/Liberty "Liberty") and advocating the establishment of an authoritarian rule by an [oligarchy](/wiki/Oligarchy "Oligarchy") set up by an unelected parliament.

Upon the [Restoration](/wiki/English_Restoration "English Restoration") in May 1660, Milton, fearing for his life, went into hiding, while a [warrant](/wiki/Warrant_(law) "Warrant (law)") was issued for his arrest and his writings were burnt. He re-emerged after [a general pardon](/wiki/Indemnity_and_Oblivion_Act "Indemnity and Oblivion Act") was issued, but was nevertheless arrested and briefly imprisoned before influential friends intervened, such as Marvell, now an MP. Milton married for a third and final time on 24 February 1663, marrying Elizabeth (Betty) Minshull, aged 24, a native of [Wistaston](/wiki/Wistaston "Wistaston"), Cheshire. He spent the remaining decade of his life living quietly in London, only retiring to a cottage during the [Great Plague of London](/wiki/Great_Plague_of_London "Great Plague of London")—[Milton's Cottage](/wiki/Milton%27s_Cottage "Milton's Cottage") in [Chalfont St. Giles](/wiki/Chalfont_St._Giles "Chalfont St. Giles"), his only extant home.

During this period, Milton published several minor prose works, such as the grammar textbook *Art of Logic* and a *History of Britain*. His only explicitly political tracts were the 1672 *Of True Religion*, arguing for [toleration](/wiki/Toleration "Toleration") (except for Catholics), and a translation of a Polish tract advocating an elective monarchy. Both these works were referred to in the [Exclusion](/wiki/Exclusion_Bill "Exclusion Bill") debate, the attempt to exclude the heir presumptive from the throne of England—[James, Duke of York](/wiki/James,_Duke_of_York "James, Duke of York")—because he was Roman Catholic. That debate preoccupied politics in the 1670s and 1680s and precipitated the formation of the [Whig party](/wiki/British_Whig_Party "British Whig Party") and the [Glorious Revolution](/wiki/Glorious_Revolution "Glorious Revolution").

Death
-----

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Milton&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Death")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2d/Milton_Statue_in_the_Church_of_Saint_Giles-without-Cripplegate_%2802%29.jpg/250px-Milton_Statue_in_the_Church_of_Saint_Giles-without-Cripplegate_%2802%29.jpg)](/wiki/File:Milton_Statue_in_the_Church_of_Saint_Giles-without-Cripplegate_(02).jpg)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c0/Milton_Memorial_in_the_Church_of_Saint_Giles-without-Cripplegate_%2802%29.jpg/250px-Milton_Memorial_in_the_Church_of_Saint_Giles-without-Cripplegate_%2802%29.jpg)](/wiki/File:Milton_Memorial_in_the_Church_of_Saint_Giles-without-Cripplegate_(02).jpg)

Milton's statue and memorial in [St Giles-without-Cripplegate](/wiki/St_Giles-without-Cripplegate "St Giles-without-Cripplegate") church, London

Milton died on 8 November 1674, a month before his 66th birth anniversary. He was buried in the church of [St Giles-without-Cripplegate](/wiki/St_Giles-without-Cripplegate "St Giles-without-Cripplegate"), [Fore Street](/wiki/Fore_Street,_London "Fore Street, London"), London.[[49]](#cite_note-Cripplegate-49) It is disputed whether the cause of death was [consumption](/wiki/Tuberculosis "Tuberculosis") or [gout](/wiki/Gout "Gout").[[49]](#cite_note-Cripplegate-49)[[50]](#cite_note-50) According to an early biographer, his funeral was attended by "his learned and great Friends in London, not without a friendly concourse of the Vulgar."[[51]](#cite_note-51) A monument was added in 1737 on Westminster Abbey in London, UK.

Family
------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Milton&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Family")]

Milton and his first wife Mary Powell (1625–1652) had four children:[[52]](#cite_note-52)

* Anne (born 29 July 1646)
* Mary (born 25 October 1648)
* John (16 March 1651 – June 1652)
* Deborah (2 May 1652 – 10 August 1727[[53]](#cite_note-53))

Mary Powell died on 5 May 1652 from complications following Deborah's birth. Milton's daughters survived to adulthood, but he always had a strained relationship with them.

On 12 November 1656, Milton was married to Katherine Woodcock at [St Margaret's, Westminster](/wiki/St_Margaret%27s,_Westminster "St Margaret's, Westminster").[[54]](#cite_note-54) She died on 3 February 1658, less than four months after giving birth to her daughter Katherine, who also died.

Milton married for a third time on 24 February 1663 to Elizabeth Mynshull or Minshull (1638–1728), the niece of Thomas Mynshull, a wealthy apothecary and philanthropist in [Manchester](/wiki/Manchester "Manchester"). The marriage took place at [St Mary Aldermary](/wiki/St_Mary_Aldermary "St Mary Aldermary") in the City of London. Despite a 30-year age gap, the marriage seemed happy, according to [John Aubrey](/wiki/John_Aubrey "John Aubrey"), and lasted more than 12 years until Milton's death. (A plaque on the wall of Mynshull's House in Manchester describes Elizabeth as Milton's "3rd and Best wife".) Samuel Johnson, however, claims that Mynshull was "a domestic companion and attendant" and Milton's nephew [Edward Phillips](/wiki/Edward_Phillips "Edward Phillips") relates that Mynshull "oppressed his children in his lifetime, and cheated them at his death".[[55]](#cite_note-55)

His nephews, [Edward](/wiki/Edward_Phillips "Edward Phillips") and [John Phillips](/wiki/John_Phillips_(author) "John Phillips (author)") (sons of Milton's sister Anne), were educated by Milton and became writers themselves. John acted as a secretary, and Edward was Milton's first biographer.

Poetry
------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Milton&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Poetry")]

Milton's poetry was slow to see the light of day, at least under his name. His first published poem was "On Shakespeare" (1630), anonymously included in the [Second Folio](/wiki/Second_Folio "Second Folio") edition of [William Shakespeare](/wiki/William_Shakespeare "William Shakespeare")'s plays in 1632. An annotated copy of the [First Folio](/wiki/First_Folio "First Folio") has been suggested to contain marginal notes by Milton.[[56]](#cite_note-56) Milton collected his work in *[1645 Poems](/wiki/1645_Poems "1645 Poems")* in the midst of the excitement attending the possibility of establishing a new English government. The anonymous edition of *Comus* was published in 1637, and the publication of *Lycidas* in 1638 in *Justa Edouardo King Naufrago* was signed J. M. Otherwise. The 1645 collection was the only poetry of his to see print until *[Paradise Lost](/wiki/Paradise_Lost "Paradise Lost")* appeared in 1667.

### *Paradise Lost*

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Milton&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Paradise Lost")]

Main article: [Paradise Lost](/wiki/Paradise_Lost "Paradise Lost")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/95/Milton_diktiert_seinen_T%C3%B6chtern_das_%C2%BBParadise_Lost%C2%AB_%28Eug%C3%A8ne_Ferdinand_Victor_Delacroix%29.jpg/250px-Milton_diktiert_seinen_T%C3%B6chtern_das_%C2%BBParadise_Lost%C2%AB_%28Eug%C3%A8ne_Ferdinand_Victor_Delacroix%29.jpg)](/wiki/File:Milton_diktiert_seinen_T%C3%B6chtern_das_%C2%BBParadise_Lost%C2%AB_(Eug%C3%A8ne_Ferdinand_Victor_Delacroix).jpg)

*Milton Dictates the Lost Paradise to His Three Daughters*, 1827 or 1828, by [Eugène Delacroix](/wiki/Eug%C3%A8ne_Delacroix "Eugène Delacroix")

Milton's *[magnum opus](/wiki/Masterpiece "Masterpiece")*, the [blank-verse](/wiki/Blank-verse "Blank-verse") [epic poem](/wiki/Epic_poetry "Epic poetry") *[Paradise Lost](/wiki/Paradise_Lost "Paradise Lost")*, was composed by the blind and impoverished Milton from 1658 to 1664 (first edition), with small but significant revisions published in 1674 (second edition). As a blind poet, Milton dictated his verse to a series of aides in his employ. It has been argued that the poem reflects his personal despair at the failure of the [Revolution](/wiki/English_Civil_War "English Civil War") yet affirms an ultimate optimism in human potential. Some literary critics have argued that Milton encoded many references to his unyielding support for the "[Good Old Cause](/wiki/Good_Old_Cause "Good Old Cause")".[[57]](#cite_note-57)

On 27 April 1667,[[58]](#cite_note-Lindenbaum1995-58) Milton sold the publication rights for *Paradise Lost* to publisher [Samuel Simmons](/wiki/Samuel_Simmons_(printer) "Samuel Simmons (printer)") for £5 (equivalent to approximately £770 in 2015 purchasing power),[[59]](#cite_note-59) with a further £5 to be paid if and when each print run sold out of between 1,300 and 1,500 copies.[[60]](#cite_note-60) The first run was a [quarto](/wiki/Bookbinding "Bookbinding") edition priced at three [shillings](/wiki/Shilling_(English_coin) "Shilling (English coin)") per copy (about £23 in 2015 purchasing power equivalent), published in August 1667, and it sold out in eighteen months.[[61]](#cite_note-61)

Milton followed up the publication *Paradise Lost* with its sequel *[Paradise Regained](/wiki/Paradise_Regained "Paradise Regained")*, which was published alongside the tragedy *[Samson Agonistes](/wiki/Samson_Agonistes "Samson Agonistes")* in 1671. Both of these works also reflect Milton's post-Restoration political situation. Just before his death in 1674, Milton supervised a second edition of *Paradise Lost*, accompanied by an explanation of "why the poem rhymes not", and prefatory verses by [Andrew Marvell](/wiki/Andrew_Marvell "Andrew Marvell"). In 1673, Milton republished his *1645 Poems*, as well as a collection of his letters and the Latin [prolusions](/w/index.php?title=Prolusion&action=edit&redlink=1 "Prolusion (page does not exist)") from his Cambridge days.

Views
-----

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Milton&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Views")]

An unfinished religious manifesto, *[De doctrina christiana](/wiki/De_Doctrina_Christiana_(Milton) "De Doctrina Christiana (Milton)")*, probably written by Milton, lays out many of his heterodox theological views, and was not discovered and published until 1823. Milton's key beliefs were idiosyncratic, not those of an identifiable group or faction, and often they go well beyond the orthodoxy of the time. Their tone, however, stemmed from the Puritan emphasis on the centrality and inviolability of conscience.[[62]](#cite_note-62) He was his own man, but he was anticipated by [Henry Robinson](/wiki/Henry_Robinson_(writer) "Henry Robinson (writer)") in *Areopagitica*.[*[clarification needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Please_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")*]

### Philosophy

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Milton&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Philosophy")]

While Milton's beliefs are generally considered to be consistent with Protestant Christianity, [Stephen M. Fallon](/wiki/Stephen_M._Fallon "Stephen M. Fallon") argues that by the late 1650s, Milton may have at least toyed with the idea of [monism](/wiki/Monism "Monism") or animist materialism, the notion that a single material substance which is "animate, self-active, and free" composes everything in the universe: from stones and trees and bodies to minds, souls, angels, and God.[[63]](#cite_note-63) Fallon claims that Milton devised this position to avoid the [mind-body dualism](/wiki/Dualism_(philosophy_of_mind) "Dualism (philosophy of mind)") of [Plato](/wiki/Plato "Plato") and [Descartes](/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Descartes "René Descartes") as well as the [mechanistic](/wiki/Mechanism_(philosophy) "Mechanism (philosophy)") [determinism](/wiki/Determinism "Determinism") of [Hobbes](/wiki/Thomas_Hobbes "Thomas Hobbes"). According to Fallon, Milton's monism is most notably reflected in *Paradise Lost* when he has angels eat (5.433–439)[*[clarification needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Please_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")*] and apparently engage in sexual intercourse (8.622–629)[*[clarification needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Please_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")*] and the *De Doctrina*, where he denies the dual natures of man and argues for a theory of Creation [*ex Deo*](/wiki/Ex_nihilo "Ex nihilo"). Fallon proposes that, in *Paradise Lost*, Milton portrays humans and angels as being composed of the same basic material, in different degrees. He cites exemplary passages from Raphael's conversation with Adam in Book V, remarking that, for Milton, heavenly spirit is only a more highly perfected expression of earthly matter. Fallon also argues that the reproductive imagery in Milton's creation scene in Book VII points to matter as being animate.[[64]](#cite_note-64)

Milton's animist monism, as outlined by Fallon, might have become compromised by an increasing skepticism towards egalitarian politics at the end of his life. John Rogers suggests that the dead matter cast away in the Creation scene of *Paradise Lost* represents an elitist break from monism and toward a hierarchical dualism between spiritual matter and its grosser counterpart.[[65]](#cite_note-:5-65)

### Political thought

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Milton&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Political thought")]

Main article: [John Milton's politics](/wiki/John_Milton%27s_politics "John Milton's politics")

Milton was a "passionately individual Christian Humanist poet."[[66]](#cite_note-:0-66) He appears on the pages of seventeenth-century English Puritanism, an age characterized as "the world turned upside down."[[67]](#cite_note-67) He was a Puritan and yet was unwilling to surrender conscience to party positions on public policy. Thus, Milton's political thought, driven by competing convictions, a Reformed faith and a Humanist spirit, led to enigmatic outcomes.

> Milton's apparently contradictory stance on the vital problems of his age, arose from religious contestations to the questions of the divine rights of kings. In both cases, he seems in control, taking stock of the situation arising from the polarization of the English society on religious and political lines. He fought with the Puritans against the Cavaliers i.e. the King's party, and helped win the day. But the very same constitutional and republican polity, when tried to curtail freedom of speech, Milton, given his humanistic zeal, wrote *Areopagitica* . . . [*sic*][[68]](#cite_note-:1-68)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a1/Areopagitica_1644bw_gobeirne.png/250px-Areopagitica_1644bw_gobeirne.png)](/wiki/File:Areopagitica_1644bw_gobeirne.png)

Title page of John Milton's 1644 edition of *[Areopagitica](/wiki/Areopagitica "Areopagitica")*

*Areopagitica* was written in response to the Licensing Order, in November 1644.[[69]](#cite_note-69)

Milton's political thought may be best categorized according to respective periods in his life and times. The years 1641–42 were dedicated to church politics and the struggle against episcopacy. After his divorce writings, *Areopagitica*, and a gap, he wrote in 1649–54 in the aftermath of the [execution of Charles I](/wiki/Execution_of_Charles_I "Execution of Charles I"), and in polemic justification of the regicide and the existing Parliamentarian regime. Then in 1659–60 he foresaw the Restoration and wrote to head it off.[[70]](#cite_note-70)

Milton's own beliefs were in some cases unpopular, particularly his commitment to [republicanism](/wiki/Republicanism "Republicanism"). In the coming centuries, Milton would be claimed as an early apostle of liberalism.[[71]](#cite_note-71) According to James Tully:

> ... with [Locke](/wiki/John_Locke "John Locke") as with Milton, republican and [contraction](/wiki/Social_contract "Social contract") conceptions of political freedom join hands in common opposition to the disengaged and passive subjection offered by [absolutists](/wiki/Absolutism_(European_history) "Absolutism (European history)") such as [Hobbes](/wiki/Thomas_Hobbes "Thomas Hobbes") and [Robert Filmer](/wiki/Robert_Filmer "Robert Filmer").[[72]](#cite_note-72)

A friend and ally in the pamphlet wars was [Marchamont Nedham](/wiki/Marchamont_Nedham "Marchamont Nedham"). [Austin Woolrych](/wiki/Austin_Woolrych "Austin Woolrych") considers that although they were quite close, there is "little real affinity, beyond a broad republicanism", between their approaches.[[73]](#cite_note-73) [Blair Worden](/wiki/Blair_Worden "Blair Worden") remarks that both Milton and Nedham, with others such as [Andrew Marvell](/wiki/Andrew_Marvell "Andrew Marvell") and [James Harrington](/wiki/James_Harrington_(author) "James Harrington (author)"), would have taken their problem with the [Rump Parliament](/wiki/Rump_Parliament "Rump Parliament") to be not the republic itself, but the fact that it was not a proper republic.[[74]](#cite_note-74) Woolrych speaks of "the gulf between Milton's vision of the Commonwealth's future and the reality".[[75]](#cite_note-75) In the early version of his *[History of Britain](/wiki/History_of_Britain_(John_Milton) "History of Britain (John Milton)")*, begun in 1649, Milton was already writing off the members of the [Long Parliament](/wiki/Long_Parliament "Long Parliament") as incorrigible.[[76]](#cite_note-76)

He praised [Oliver Cromwell](/wiki/Oliver_Cromwell "Oliver Cromwell") as the Protectorate was set up; though subsequently he had major reservations. When Cromwell seemed to be backsliding as a revolutionary, after a couple of years in power, Milton moved closer to the position of [Sir Henry Vane](/wiki/Henry_Vane_the_Younger "Henry Vane the Younger"), to whom he wrote a sonnet in 1652.[[77]](#cite_note-77)[[78]](#cite_note-78) The group of disaffected republicans included, besides Vane, [John Bradshaw](/wiki/John_Bradshaw_(judge) "John Bradshaw (judge)"), [John Hutchinson](/wiki/John_Hutchinson_(Colonel) "John Hutchinson (Colonel)"), [Edmund Ludlow](/wiki/Edmund_Ludlow "Edmund Ludlow"), [Henry Marten](/wiki/Henry_Marten_(regicide) "Henry Marten (regicide)"), [Robert Overton](/wiki/Robert_Overton "Robert Overton"), [Edward Sexby](/wiki/Edward_Sexby "Edward Sexby") and [John Streater](/wiki/John_Streater "John Streater"); but not Marvell, who remained with Cromwell's party.[[79]](#cite_note-79) Milton had already commended Overton, along with [Edmund Whalley](/wiki/Edmund_Whalley "Edmund Whalley") and [Bulstrode Whitelocke](/wiki/Bulstrode_Whitelocke "Bulstrode Whitelocke"), in *[Defensio Secunda](/wiki/Defensio_Secunda "Defensio Secunda")*.[[80]](#cite_note-80) Nigel Smith writes that

> ... John Streater, and the form of republicanism he stood for, was a fulfilment of Milton's most optimistic ideas of free speech and of public heroism [...][[81]](#cite_note-81)

As [Richard Cromwell](/wiki/Richard_Cromwell "Richard Cromwell") fell from power, he envisaged a step towards a freer republic or "free commonwealth", writing in the hope of this outcome in early 1660. Milton had argued for an awkward position, in the *[Ready and Easy Way](/wiki/The_Ready_and_Easy_Way_to_Establish_a_Free_Commonwealth "The Ready and Easy Way to Establish a Free Commonwealth")*, because he wanted to invoke the [Good Old Cause](/wiki/Good_Old_Cause "Good Old Cause") and gain the support of the republicans, but without offering a democratic solution of any kind.[[82]](#cite_note-82) His proposal, backed by reference (amongst other reasons) to the [oligarchical](/wiki/Oligarchical "Oligarchical") Dutch and Venetian constitutions, was for a council with perpetual membership. This attitude cut right across the grain of popular opinion of the time, which swung decisively behind the restoration of the Stuart monarchy that took place later in the year.[[83]](#cite_note-83) Milton, an associate of and advocate on behalf of the regicides, was silenced on political matters as Charles II returned.

John Rogers has argued that Milton's views became more elitist after his early pamphlets. Losing faith in popular democracy, he began to favor government by a minority of competent citizens.[[84]](#cite_note-:4-84) Rogers presents this change as evident in *Paradise Lost*. God's choice to use armed force against disobedient subjects echoes Milton's own endorsement of military suppression against the majority in the *Ready and Easy Way*.[[84]](#cite_note-:4-84) The shift towards elitism is interpreted as a response to the immovable conservatism of Milton's English contemporaries, to whom Milton referred in increasingly condescending terms.[[65]](#cite_note-:5-65)

### Theology

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Milton&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Theology")]

Main article: [John Milton's religion](/wiki/John_Milton%27s_religion "John Milton's religion")

John Milton was neither a clergyman nor a theologian; however, theology, and particularly English Calvinism, formed the palette on which he created his greatest thoughts. Milton wrestled with the great doctrines of the Church amidst the theological crosswinds of his age. The great poet was undoubtedly Reformed (though his grandfather, Richard "the Ranger" Milton had been Roman Catholic).[[85]](#cite_note-:2-85)[[7]](#cite_note-:3-7) However, Milton's Calvinism had to find expression in a broad-spirited Humanism. Like many [Renaissance](/wiki/Renaissance "Renaissance") artists before him, Milton attempted to integrate Christian theology with classical modes. In his early poems, the poet narrator expresses a tension between vice and virtue, the latter invariably related to Protestantism. In *Comus*, Milton may make ironic use of the [Caroline](/wiki/Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England") court [masque](/wiki/Masque "Masque") by elevating notions of purity and virtue over the conventions of court revelry and superstition. In his later poems, Milton's theological concerns become more explicit.

His use of biblical citation was wide-ranging; Harris Fletcher, standing at the beginning of the intensification of the study of the use of scripture in Milton's work (poetry and prose, in all languages Milton mastered), notes that typically Milton clipped and adapted biblical quotations to suit the purpose, giving precise chapter and verse only in texts for a more specialized readership. As for the plenitude of Milton's quotations from scripture, Fletcher comments, "For this work, I have in all actually collated about twenty-five hundred of the five to ten thousand direct Biblical quotations which appear therein".[[86]](#cite_note-harris-86) Milton's customary English Bible was the [Authorized King James](/wiki/King_James_Version#Authorized_Version "King James Version").[[87]](#cite_note-87) When citing and writing in other languages, he usually employed the Latin translation by [Immanuel Tremellius](/wiki/Immanuel_Tremellius "Immanuel Tremellius"), though "he was equipped to read the Bible in Latin, in Greek, and in Hebrew, including the Targumim or Aramaic paraphrases of the Old Testament, and the Syriac version of the New, together with the available commentaries of those several versions".[[86]](#cite_note-harris-86)

Milton embraced many heterodox Christian theological views. He has been accused of rejecting the [Trinity](/wiki/Trinity "Trinity"), believing instead that the Son was subordinate to the Father, a position known as [Arianism](/wiki/Arianism "Arianism"); and his sympathy or curiosity was probably engaged by [Socinianism](/wiki/Socinianism "Socinianism"): in August 1650 he licensed for publication by [William Dugard](/wiki/William_Dugard "William Dugard") the *[Racovian Catechism](/wiki/Racovian_Catechism "Racovian Catechism")*, based on a non-trinitarian creed.[[88]](#cite_note-88)[[89]](#cite_note-89) Milton's alleged Arianism, like much of his theology, is still the subject of debate and controversy. [Rufus Wilmot Griswold](/wiki/Rufus_Wilmot_Griswold "Rufus Wilmot Griswold") argued that "In none of his great works is there a passage from which it can be inferred that he was an Arian; and in the very last of his writings he declares that "the doctrine of the Trinity is a plain doctrine in Scripture."[[90]](#cite_note-90) In *Areopagitica,* Milton classified Arians and Socinians as "errorists" and "schismatics" alongside [Arminians](/wiki/Arminians "Arminians") and [Anabaptists](/wiki/Anabaptists "Anabaptists").[[91]](#cite_note-91) A source has interpreted him as broadly Protestant, if not always easy to locate in a more precise religious category. In 2019, John Rogers stated, "Heretics both, John Milton and Isaac Newton were, as most scholars now agree, Arians."[[92]](#cite_note-92)[[93]](#cite_note-heretic-93)

In his 1641 treatise, *[Of Reformation](/wiki/Of_Reformation "Of Reformation")*, Milton expressed his dislike for Catholicism and episcopacy, presenting Rome as a modern [Babylon](/wiki/Babylon "Babylon"), and bishops as Egyptian taskmasters. These analogies conform to Milton's puritanical preference for [Old Testament](/wiki/Old_Testament "Old Testament") imagery. He knew at least four commentaries on *Genesis*: those of [John Calvin](/wiki/John_Calvin "John Calvin"), [Paulus Fagius](/wiki/Paulus_Fagius "Paulus Fagius"), [David Pareus](/wiki/David_Pareus "David Pareus") and [Andreus Rivetus](/wiki/Andreus_Rivetus "Andreus Rivetus").[[94]](#cite_note-94)

Through the [Interregnum](/wiki/Interregnum_(1649%E2%80%931660) "Interregnum (1649–1660)"), Milton often presents England, rescued from the trappings of a worldly monarchy, as an [elect](/wiki/Elect "Elect") nation akin to the Old Testament [Israel](/wiki/Israel "Israel"), and shows its leader, [Oliver Cromwell](/wiki/Oliver_Cromwell "Oliver Cromwell"), as a latter-day [Moses](/wiki/Moses "Moses"). These views were bound up in Protestant views of the [Millennium](/wiki/Millennialism "Millennialism"), which some sects, such as the [Fifth Monarchists](/wiki/Fifth_Monarchists "Fifth Monarchists") predicted would arrive in England. Milton, however, would later criticise the "worldly" millenarian views of these and others, and expressed orthodox ideas on the prophecy of the [Four Empires](/wiki/Four_Empires "Four Empires").[[95]](#cite_note-95)

The Restoration of the Stuart monarchy in 1660 began a new phase in Milton's work. In *Paradise Lost*, *[Paradise Regained](/wiki/Paradise_Regained "Paradise Regained")* and *[Samson Agonistes](/wiki/Samson_Agonistes "Samson Agonistes")*, Milton mourns the end of the godly [Commonwealth](/wiki/English_Commonwealth "English Commonwealth"). The [Garden of Eden](/wiki/Garden_of_Eden "Garden of Eden") may allegorically reflect Milton's view of England's recent [Fall from Grace](/wiki/The_Fall_of_Man "The Fall of Man"), while [Samson](/wiki/Samson "Samson")'s blindness and captivity—mirroring Milton's own lost sight—may be a metaphor for England's blind acceptance of [Charles II](/wiki/Charles_II_of_England "Charles II of England") as king. Illustrated by *Paradise Lost* is [mortalism](/wiki/Soul_sleep "Soul sleep"), the belief that the soul lies dormant after the body dies.[[96]](#cite_note-96)

Despite the Restoration of the monarchy, Milton did not lose his personal faith; *Samson* shows how the loss of national [salvation](/wiki/Salvation "Salvation") did not necessarily preclude the salvation of the individual, while *Paradise Regained* expresses Milton's continuing belief in the promise of Christian salvation through Jesus Christ.

Though he maintained his personal faith in spite of the defeats suffered by his cause, the *[Dictionary of National Biography](/wiki/Dictionary_of_National_Biography "Dictionary of National Biography")* recounted how he had been alienated from the Church of England by Archbishop William Laud, and then moved similarly from the [Dissenters](/wiki/Dissenters "Dissenters") by their denunciation of religious tolerance in England.

> Milton had come to stand apart from all sects, though apparently finding the [Quakers](/wiki/Quakers "Quakers") most congenial. He never went to any religious services in his later years. When a servant brought back accounts of sermons from [nonconformist](/wiki/Nonconformist_(Protestantism) "Nonconformist (Protestantism)") meetings, Milton became so sarcastic that the man at last gave up his place.

Writing of the enigmatic and often conflicting views of Milton in the Puritan age, David Daiches wrote,

> "Christian and Humanist, Protestant, patriot and heir of the golden ages of Greece and Rome, he faced what appeared to him to be the birth-pangs of a new and regenerate England with high excitement and idealistic optimism."[[66]](#cite_note-:0-66)

A fair theological summary may be that John Milton was a Puritan, though his tendency to press further for liberty of conscience, sometimes out of conviction and often out of mere intellectual curiosity, made the great man, at least, a vital if not uncomfortable ally in the broader Puritan movement.[[68]](#cite_note-:1-68)[[85]](#cite_note-:2-85)

### Religious toleration

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Milton&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Religious toleration")]

Milton called in the *[Areopagitica](/wiki/Areopagitica "Areopagitica")* for "the liberty to know, to utter, and to argue freely according to conscience, above all liberties" to the conflicting Protestant denominations.[[97]](#cite_note-97) According to American historian William Hunter, "Milton argued for [disestablishment](/wiki/Disestablishment "Disestablishment") as the only effective way of achieving broad [toleration](/wiki/Religious_toleration "Religious toleration"). Rather than force a man's conscience, government should recognise the persuasive force of the gospel."[[98]](#cite_note-98)

### Divorce

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Milton&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Divorce")]

Main article: [Milton's divorce tracts](/wiki/Milton%27s_divorce_tracts "Milton's divorce tracts")

Milton wrote *The Doctrine and Discipline of Divorce* in 1643, at the beginning of the English Civil War. In August of that year, he presented his thoughts to the [Westminster Assembly of Divines](/wiki/Westminster_Assembly_of_Divines "Westminster Assembly of Divines"), which had been created by the [Long Parliament](/wiki/Long_Parliament "Long Parliament") to bring greater reform to the Church of England. The Assembly convened on 1 July against the will of King Charles I.

Milton's thinking on divorce caused him considerable trouble with the authorities. An orthodox Presbyterian view of the time was that Milton's views on divorce constituted a one-man [heresy](/wiki/Heresy "Heresy"):

> The fervently Presbyterian [Edwards](/wiki/Thomas_Edwards_(heresiographer) "Thomas Edwards (heresiographer)") had included Milton's divorce tracts in his list in *[Gangraena](/wiki/Gangraena "Gangraena")* of heretical publications that threatened the religious and moral fabric of the nation; Milton responded by mocking him as "shallow Edwards" in the satirical sonnet "On the New Forcers of Conscience under the Long Parliament", usually dated to the latter half of 1646.[[99]](#cite_note-99)

Even here, though, his originality is qualified: [Thomas Gataker](/wiki/Thomas_Gataker "Thomas Gataker") had already identified "mutual solace" as a principal goal in marriage.[[100]](#cite_note-100) Milton abandoned his campaign to legitimise divorce after 1645, but he expressed support for [polygamy](/wiki/Polygamy "Polygamy") in the *[De Doctrina Christiana](/wiki/De_Doctrina_Christiana_(Milton) "De Doctrina Christiana (Milton)")*, the theological treatise that provides the clearest evidence for his views.[[101]](#cite_note-101)

Milton wrote during a period when thoughts about divorce were anything but simplistic; rather, there was active debate among thinkers and intellectuals at the time. However, Milton's basic approval of divorce within strict parameters set by the biblical witness was typical of many influential Christian intellectuals, particularly the Westminster divines. Milton addressed the Assembly on the matter of divorce in August 1643,[[102]](#cite_note-102) at a moment when the Assembly was beginning to form its opinion on the matter. In the *Doctrine and Discipline of Divorce*, Milton argued that divorce was a private matter, not a legal or ecclesiastical one. Neither the Assembly nor Parliament condemned Milton or his ideas. In fact, when the Westminster Assembly wrote the Westminster Confession of Faith they allowed for divorce ('Of Marriage and Divorce,' Chapter 24, Section 5) in cases of infidelity or abandonment. Thus, the Christian community, at least a majority within the 'Puritan' sub-set, approved of Milton's views.

Nevertheless, the reaction among Puritans to Milton's views on divorce was mixed. [Herbert Palmer](/wiki/Herbert_Palmer_(Puritan) "Herbert Palmer (Puritan)"), a member of the Westminster Assembly, condemned Milton in the strongest possible language:

> If any plead Conscience ... for divorce for other causes than Christ and His Apostles mention; Of which a wicked booke is abroad and uncensured, though deserving to be burnt, whose Author, hath been so impudent as to set his Name to it, and dedicate it to your selves ... will you grant a Toleration for all this?

— *The Glasse of God's Providence Towards His Faithfull Ones*, 1644, p. 54.[[103]](#cite_note-103)

Palmer expressed his disapproval in a sermon addressed to the Westminster Assembly. The Scottish commissioner Robert Baillie described Palmer's sermon as one "of the most Scottish and free sermons that ever I heard anywhere".[[104]](#cite_note-104)

### History

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Milton&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: History")]

History was particularly important for the political class of the period, and Lewalski considers that Milton "more than most illustrates" a remark of [Thomas Hobbes](/wiki/Thomas_Hobbes "Thomas Hobbes") on the weight placed at the time on the classical Latin historical writers [Tacitus](/wiki/Tacitus "Tacitus"), [Livy](/wiki/Livy "Livy"), [Sallust](/wiki/Sallust "Sallust") and [Cicero](/wiki/Cicero "Cicero"), and their republican attitudes.[[105]](#cite_note-105) Milton himself wrote that "Worthy deeds are not often destitute of worthy relaters", in Book II of his *History of Britain*. A sense of history mattered greatly to him:[[106]](#cite_note-106)

> The course of human history, the immediate impact of the civil disorders, and his own traumatic personal life, are all regarded by Milton as typical of the predicament he describes as "the misery that has bin since Adam".[[107]](#cite_note-107)

Legacy and influence
--------------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Milton&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Legacy and influence")]

Once *Paradise Lost* was published, Milton's stature as an epic poet was immediately recognised. He cast a formidable shadow over English poetry in the 18th and 19th centuries; he was often judged equal or superior to all other English poets, including [Shakespeare](/wiki/Shakespeare "Shakespeare"). Very early on, though, he was championed by [Whigs](/wiki/Whig_(British_political_faction) "Whig (British political faction)"), and decried by [Tories](/wiki/Tories_(British_political_party) "Tories (British political party)"): with the regicide [Edmund Ludlow](/wiki/Edmund_Ludlow "Edmund Ludlow") he was claimed as an early Whig,[[108]](#cite_note-108) while the High Tory Anglican minister [Luke Milbourne](/wiki/Luke_Milbourne "Luke Milbourne") lumped Milton in with other "Agents of Darkness" such as [John Knox](/wiki/John_Knox "John Knox"), [George Buchanan](/wiki/George_Buchanan "George Buchanan"), [Richard Baxter](/wiki/Richard_Baxter "Richard Baxter"), [Algernon Sidney](/wiki/Algernon_Sidney "Algernon Sidney") and [John Locke](/wiki/John_Locke "John Locke").[[109]](#cite_note-109) The political ideas of Milton, Locke, Sidney, and [James Harrington](/wiki/James_Harrington_(author) "James Harrington (author)") strongly influenced the [Radical Whigs](/wiki/Radical_Whigs "Radical Whigs"), whose ideology in turn was central to the [American Revolution](/wiki/American_Revolution "American Revolution").[[110]](#cite_note-110) Modern scholars of Milton's life, politics, and work are known as Miltonists: "his work is the subject of a very large amount of academic scholarship".[[111]](#cite_note-111)

In 2008, John Milton Passage, a short passage by Bread Street into St Mary-le-Bow Churchyard in London, was unveiled.[[112]](#cite_note-112)

### Early reception of the poetry

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Milton&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Early reception of the poetry")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/02/MiltonPoeticalWorksNewton1752-61.jpg/250px-MiltonPoeticalWorksNewton1752-61.jpg)](/wiki/File:MiltonPoeticalWorksNewton1752-61.jpg)

Title page of a 1752–1761 edition of "The Poetical Works of John Milton with Notes of Various Authors by Thomas Newton" printed by J. & R. Tonson in the Strand

[John Dryden](/wiki/John_Dryden "John Dryden"), an early enthusiast, in 1677 began the trend of describing Milton as the poet of the [sublime](/wiki/Sublime_(philosophy) "Sublime (philosophy)").[[113]](#cite_note-113) Dryden's *The State of Innocence and the Fall of Man: an Opera* (1677) is evidence of an immediate cultural influence. In 1695, [Patrick Hume](/wiki/Patrick_Hume_(editor) "Patrick Hume (editor)") became the first editor of *Paradise Lost*, providing an extensive apparatus of annotation and commentary, particularly chasing down allusions.[[114]](#cite_note-114)

In 1732, the classical scholar [Richard Bentley](/wiki/Richard_Bentley "Richard Bentley") offered a corrected version of *Paradise Lost*.[[115]](#cite_note-115) Bentley was considered presumptuous and was attacked in the following year by [Zachary Pearce](/wiki/Zachary_Pearce "Zachary Pearce"). [Christopher Ricks](/wiki/Christopher_Ricks "Christopher Ricks") judges that, as a critic, Bentley was both acute and wrong-headed, and "incorrigibly eccentric"; [William Empson](/wiki/William_Empson "William Empson") also finds Pearce to be more sympathetic to Bentley's underlying line of thought than is warranted.[[116]](#cite_note-116)[[117]](#cite_note-117)

There was an early, partial translation of *Paradise Lost* into German by [Theodore Haak](/wiki/Theodore_Haak "Theodore Haak") and based on that a standard verse translation by Ernest Gottlieb von Berge. A subsequent prose translation by [Johann Jakob Bodmer](/wiki/Johann_Jakob_Bodmer "Johann Jakob Bodmer") was very popular; it influenced Friedrich Gottlieb Klopstock. The German-language Milton tradition returned to England in the person of the artist [Henry Fuseli](/wiki/Henry_Fuseli "Henry Fuseli").

Many Enlightenment thinkers of the 18th century revered and commented on Milton's poetry and non-poetical works. In addition to John Dryden, among them were [Alexander Pope](/wiki/Alexander_Pope "Alexander Pope"), [Joseph Addison](/wiki/Joseph_Addison "Joseph Addison"), [Thomas Newton](/wiki/Thomas_Newton "Thomas Newton"), and [Samuel Johnson](/wiki/Samuel_Johnson "Samuel Johnson"). For example, in *[The Spectator](/wiki/The_Spectator_(1711) "The Spectator (1711)")*,[[118]](#cite_note-118) Joseph Addison wrote extensive notes, annotations, and interpretations of certain passages of *Paradise Lost*. [Jonathan Richardson, senior](/wiki/Jonathan_Richardson_(painter) "Jonathan Richardson (painter)"), and Jonathan Richardson, the younger, co-wrote a book of criticism.[[119]](#cite_note-119) In 1749, Thomas Newton published an extensive edition of Milton's poetical works with annotations provided by himself, Dryden, Pope, Addison, the Richardsons (father and son) and others. Newton's edition of Milton was a culmination of the honour bestowed upon Milton by early Enlightenment thinkers; it may also have been prompted by Richard Bentley's infamous edition, described above. Samuel Johnson wrote numerous essays on *Paradise Lost*, and Milton was included in his *[Lives of the Most Eminent English Poets](/wiki/Lives_of_the_Most_Eminent_English_Poets "Lives of the Most Eminent English Poets")* (1779–1781). In *[The Age of Louis XIV](/wiki/The_Age_of_Louis_XIV "The Age of Louis XIV")*, [Voltaire](/wiki/Voltaire "Voltaire") said "Milton remains the glory and the wonder (*l'admiration*) of England."[[120]](#cite_note-120)

### William Blake

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Milton&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: William Blake")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3b/Milton_a_Poem_copy_D_1818_Library_of_Congress_object_1.jpg/250px-Milton_a_Poem_copy_D_1818_Library_of_Congress_object_1.jpg)](/wiki/File:Milton_a_Poem_copy_D_1818_Library_of_Congress_object_1.jpg)

[Frontispiece](/wiki/Frontispiece_(book) "Frontispiece (book)") to *[Milton: A Poem in Two Books](/wiki/Milton:_A_Poem_in_Two_Books "Milton: A Poem in Two Books")*

[William Blake](/wiki/William_Blake "William Blake") considered Milton the major English poet. Blake placed [Edmund Spenser](/wiki/Edmund_Spenser "Edmund Spenser") as Milton's precursor, and saw himself as Milton's poetical son.[[121]](#cite_note-121) In his *[Milton: A Poem in Two Books](/wiki/Milton:_A_Poem_in_Two_Books "Milton: A Poem in Two Books")*, Blake uses Milton as a spiritual guide and a symbol of poetic inspiration.[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

### Romantic theory

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Milton&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Romantic theory")]

[Edmund Burke](/wiki/Edmund_Burke "Edmund Burke") was a theorist of the [sublime](/wiki/Sublime_(literary) "Sublime (literary)"), and he regarded Milton's description of Hell as exemplary of sublimity as an [aesthetic](/wiki/Aesthetics "Aesthetics") concept. For Burke, it was to set alongside mountaintops, a storm at sea, and [infinity](/wiki/Infinity "Infinity").[[122]](#cite_note-122) In *The Beautiful and the Sublime*, he wrote: "No person seems better to have understood the secret of heightening, or of setting terrible things, if I may use the expression, in their strongest light, by the force of a judicious obscurity than Milton."[[123]](#cite_note-123)

The [Romantic poets](/wiki/Romanticism "Romanticism") valued his exploration of [blank verse](/wiki/Blank_verse "Blank verse"), but for the most part rejected his religiosity. [William Wordsworth](/wiki/William_Wordsworth "William Wordsworth") began his sonnet "London, 1802" with "Milton! thou should'st be living at this hour"[[124]](#cite_note-124) and modelled *[The Prelude](/wiki/The_Prelude "The Prelude")*, his own blank verse epic, on *Paradise Lost*. [John Keats](/wiki/John_Keats "John Keats") found the yoke of Milton's style uncongenial;[[125]](#cite_note-125) he exclaimed that "[Miltonic verse](/wiki/Miltonic_verse "Miltonic verse") cannot be written but in an artful or rather artist's humour."[[126]](#cite_note-Leader-126) Keats felt that *Paradise Lost* was a "beautiful and grand curiosity", but his own unfinished attempt at epic poetry, *[Hyperion](/wiki/Hyperion_(poem) "Hyperion (poem)")*, was unsatisfactory to the author because, amongst other things, it had too many "Miltonic inversions".[[126]](#cite_note-Leader-126) In *[The Madwoman in the Attic](/wiki/The_Madwoman_in_the_Attic "The Madwoman in the Attic")*, [Sandra Gilbert](/wiki/Sandra_Gilbert "Sandra Gilbert") and [Susan Gubar](/wiki/Susan_Gubar "Susan Gubar") note that [Mary Shelley](/wiki/Mary_Shelley "Mary Shelley")'s novel *[Frankenstein](/wiki/Frankenstein "Frankenstein")* is, in the view of many critics, "one of the key 'Romantic' readings of *Paradise Lost*."[[127]](#cite_note-127)

### Later legacy

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Milton&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Later legacy")]

The Victorian age witnessed a continuation of Milton's influence. [Thomas Carlyle](/wiki/Thomas_Carlyle "Thomas Carlyle") declared him the "moral king of English literature,"[[128]](#cite_note-128) while [George Eliot](/wiki/George_Eliot "George Eliot")[[129]](#cite_note-129) and [Thomas Hardy](/wiki/Thomas_Hardy "Thomas Hardy") were particularly inspired by Milton's poetry and biography. Hostile 20th-century criticism by [T. S. Eliot](/wiki/T._S._Eliot "T. S. Eliot") and [Ezra Pound](/wiki/Ezra_Pound "Ezra Pound") did not reduce Milton's stature.[[130]](#cite_note-130) [F. R. Leavis](/wiki/F._R._Leavis "F. R. Leavis"), in *The Common Pursuit*, responded to the points made by Eliot, in particular the claim that "the study of Milton could be of no help: it was only a hindrance", by arguing, "As if it were a matter of deciding *not* to study Milton! The problem, rather, was to escape from an influence that was so difficult to escape from because it was unrecognized, belonging, as it did, to the climate of the habitual and 'natural'."[[131]](#cite_note-131) [Harold Bloom](/wiki/Harold_Bloom "Harold Bloom"), in *[The Anxiety of Influence](/wiki/The_Anxiety_of_Influence "The Anxiety of Influence")*, wrote that "Milton is the central problem in any theory and history of poetic influence in English [...]".[[132]](#cite_note-132)

Milton's *[Areopagitica](/wiki/Areopagitica "Areopagitica")* is still cited as relevant to the [First Amendment to the United States Constitution](/wiki/First_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution "First Amendment to the United States Constitution").[[133]](#cite_note-133) A quotation from *Areopagitica*—"A good book is the precious lifeblood of a master spirit, embalmed and treasured up on purpose to a life beyond life"—is displayed in many public libraries, including the [New York Public Library](/wiki/New_York_Public_Library "New York Public Library").

The title of [Philip Pullman](/wiki/Philip_Pullman "Philip Pullman")'s *[His Dark Materials](/wiki/His_Dark_Materials "His Dark Materials")* trilogy is derived from a quotation, "His dark materials to create more worlds", line 915 of Book II in *Paradise Lost*. Pullman was concerned to produce a version of Milton's poem accessible to teenagers,[[134]](#cite_note-134) and has spoken of Milton as "our greatest public poet".[[135]](#cite_note-135)
